questions.explanation: After a negative adverb like 'seldom' at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject: Seldom have I seen.

wrongReasons.did: With the present perfect the auxiliary is 'have', not 'did'.

questions.text: Seldom ___ I seen such a beautiful view.

questions.explanation: In a cleft sentence we use 'that' (or 'where' for places) to introduce the focused information.

wrongReasons.which: 'which' is used for things, not for a place focused in a cleft sentence.

questions.text: It was in Paris ___ they first met.

questions.explanation: After 'Never before' at the start, the auxiliary goes before the subject; 'as it has this summer' shows the present perfect: Never before has it been so busy.

wrongReasons.did: 'did' is followed by a base form, but 'seen' is a past participle, so we need 'has'.
wrongReasons.had: 'had' refers to a time before another past moment, but 'as it has this summer' shows we are talking up to now.

questions.text: Never before ___ the city seen so many tourists as it has this summer.

questions.explanation: In an it-cleft about a person we use 'who' or 'that' after the focused noun: It was Tom who called.

wrongReasons.which: 'which' refers to things, not to a person like 'my grandmother'.
wrongReasons.whom: 'whom' is an object form, but here the person is the subject of 'taught'.

questions.text: It was my grandmother ___ taught me how to bake bread.

questions.explanation: A mixed conditional uses 'If + past perfect' for the past and 'would + base form' for now: If I had saved, I would be rich now.

wrongReasons.have: The condition is about the past, so it needs the past perfect 'had studied'.
wrongReasons.would have: 'would' is not used in the if-clause; the condition needs 'had'.

questions.text: If I ___ studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.

questions.explanation: We say 'cast/throw doubt on something': The report casts doubt on his story.

wrongReasons.makes: We do not say 'make doubts on'; the collocation is 'cast doubt on'.
wrongReasons.puts: 'put doubts on' is not a natural collocation; we say 'cast doubt on'.

questions.text: The new evidence ___ serious doubts on the official version of events.

questions.explanation: 'Further to' is a formal way to refer to a previous contact: Further to your email, I attach the file.

wrongReasons.according: 'According to' introduces a source of information, not a previous contact.
wrongReasons.furthermore: 'Furthermore' adds a new point and is not followed by 'to'.

questions.text: ___ to our telephone conversation yesterday, I am writing to confirm the details.

questions.explanation: 'Having + past participle' shows one action was completed before another: Having eaten, we left.

wrongReasons.had: 'Had finished her report' without a subject is not a complete clause; use 'Having'.
wrongReasons.being: 'Being finished' would be passive and does not fit with an object ('her report').

questions.text: ___ finished her report, she went home.

questions.explanation: 'Hardly ... when' is used with the past perfect and inversion: Hardly had we left when it rained.

wrongReasons.did: 'begun' is a past participle, so it; 'Hardly ... when' needs the past perfect 'had'.
wrongReasons.has: The phone 'rang' in the past, so the earlier action needs the past perfect, not the present perfect.

questions.text: Hardly ___ the orchestra begun the overture when a phone rang in the audience.

questions.explanation: In a wh-cleft, 'What ...' is followed by a singular 'is/was': What I want is some peace.

wrongReasons.are: A 'What' clause is treated as singular, so we need 'is'.
wrongReasons.it is: 'What I need right now' is already the subject, so no extra 'it' is needed.

questions.text: What I need right now ___ a long holiday.

questions.explanation: A mixed conditional can use a present condition with a past result: If he were wiser, he would have listened.

wrongReasons.will: 'will have accepted' does not fit an unreal condition; we need 'would'.
wrongReasons.had: 'had have' is wrong; the result clause uses 'would have' + participle.

questions.text: If she weren't so stubborn, she ___ have accepted the offer last week.

questions.explanation: We 'make', 'take' or 'reach' a decision: They reached a decision quickly.

wrongReasons.do: We never say 'do a decision'; use 'make' or 'reach'.
wrongReasons.have: 'have a decision' is not a collocation; we 'make' or 'reach' a decision.

questions.text: The committee will ___ a decision by the end of the month.

questions.explanation: 'With regard to' is a formal way to say 'about': With regard to your request, ...

wrongReasons.about: 'about regard to' is wrong; the formal phrase is 'with regard to'.
wrongReasons.for: 'for regard to' is not English; use 'with regard to'.

questions.text: I am writing ___ regard to the position advertised on your website.

questions.explanation: A present participle can replace a relative clause: The man sitting there (= who was sitting there).

wrongReasons.sat: 'sat' is a past form; to mean 'who was sitting' we use 'sitting'.
wrongReasons.sits: 'sits' is a finite verb and cannot follow 'The man' directly as a description.

questions.text: The man ___ next to me on the train was reading a fascinating book.

questions.explanation: 'No sooner' is always paired with 'than': No sooner had I arrived than the phone rang.

wrongReasons.when: 'when' goes with 'Hardly' or 'Scarcely', but 'No sooner' needs 'than'.
wrongReasons.then: 'then' is an adverb of time; the fixed pattern is 'No sooner ... than'.

questions.text: No sooner had the referee blown the final whistle ___ the fans rushed onto the pitch.

questions.explanation: A wh-cleft starts with 'What' (= the thing that): What I enjoy is cooking.

wrongReasons.that: 'That I like most' cannot work as a subject here; we need 'What' (= the thing which).
wrongReasons.which: 'Which' needs a noun before it; to mean 'the thing that' we use 'What'.

questions.text: ___ I like most about this city is its architecture.

questions.explanation: 'Provided (that)' means 'only if': Provided that you pay, you can enter.

wrongReasons.if: 'Provided if' is wrong; we say 'provided that' or 'provided'.
wrongReasons.when: 'Provided when' is not a correct pattern; use 'provided that'.

questions.text: Provided ___ the funding is approved, construction will begin in the spring.

questions.explanation: We 'make' or 'leave' an impression on someone: She made a great impression.

wrongReasons.did: We don't say 'do an impression on'; it is 'make an impression'.
wrongReasons.gave: 'give an impression on' is wrong; we say 'make/leave an impression on'.

questions.text: Her speech ___ a lasting impression on the audience.

questions.explanation: 'Refrain from + -ing' is a formal way to say 'do not': Please refrain from talking.

wrongReasons.avoid: 'avoid' takes the -ing form directly (avoid taking), without 'from'.
wrongReasons.stop: 'stop from taking' is wrong here; 'stop' is followed directly by -ing.

questions.text: Spectators are asked to ___ from taking flash photographs during the performance.

questions.explanation: A past participle clause has a passive meaning: Built in 1850 = It was built in 1850.

wrongReasons.building: The bridge did not build anything; the meaning is passive, so use 'Built'.
wrongReasons.having built: 'Having built' is active, but the bridge was built by someone else.

questions.text: ___ in 1850, the bridge is one of the oldest in the country.

questions.explanation: After 'Not only' at the start we invert with an auxiliary; with a past simple meaning we use 'did' + base form: Not only did he sing, he also danced.

wrongReasons.had: 'had' would need a past participle (written), but the verb here is the base form 'write'.
wrongReasons.was: 'was' cannot be followed by the base form 'write'; we need 'did'.

questions.text: Not only ___ she write the novel, but she also designed its cover.

questions.explanation: The pattern is 'It was not until + time + that': It wasn't until June that we met.

wrongReasons.when: The fixed cleft pattern is 'It wasn't until ... that', not 'when'.
wrongReasons.than: 'than' is used in comparisons; this pattern needs 'that'.

questions.text: It wasn't until midnight ___ the results were announced.

questions.explanation: 'But for + noun' means 'if it had not been for': But for the map, we would have got lost.

wrongReasons.without: 'But without' is not a fixed form; the expression is 'But for'.
wrongReasons.of: 'But of' has no meaning here; the correct expression is 'But for'.

questions.text: But ___ your help, I would never have finished the project.

questions.explanation: We 'make' or 'turn' a profit: The shop made a profit last year.

wrongReasons.done: We don't 'do a profit'; the verb is 'make'.
wrongReasons.won: We 'win' a prize, not a profit.

questions.text: The company has ___ a profit for the first time in five years.

questions.explanation: 'I would be grateful if you could ...' is a polite formal request: I would be grateful if you could reply.

wrongReasons.that: In this formal request we use 'if', not 'that', before 'you could'.
wrongReasons.when: 'when' refers to time; a polite request uses 'if'.

questions.text: We would be grateful ___ you could complete the enclosed questionnaire.

questions.explanation: 'Not + -ing' gives a reason in a participle clause: Not having a car, I walk.

wrongReasons.known: 'Not known' is passive and does not fit; he did not know, so use 'knowing'.
wrongReasons.know: After 'Not' at the start of this clause we need the -ing form.

questions.text: Not ___ what to say, he remained silent.

questions.explanation: After 'Under no circumstances' the auxiliary comes before the subject; here it is a present passive: Under no circumstances are pets allowed.

wrongReasons.is: The subject 'employees' is plural, so the verb must be 'are'.
wrongReasons.do: 'permitted' is a passive participle, so we need the verb 'be', not 'do'.

questions.text: Under no circumstances ___ employees permitted to share their login details.

questions.explanation: 'All + clause' works like a wh-cleft and takes a singular verb: All I need is time.

wrongReasons.were: 'All she wanted' means 'the only thing she wanted', so it takes a singular verb.
wrongReasons.is: The verb 'wanted' is past, so the cleft verb should also be past: 'was'.

questions.text: All she wanted ___ to be left alone.

questions.explanation: 'If it hadn't been for + noun' means 'without' in the past: If it hadn't been for you, I would have failed.

wrongReasons.wasn't: With 'been' we need the past perfect 'hadn't', not 'wasn't'.
wrongReasons.weren't: 'weren't been' is not correct; the form is 'hadn't been'.

questions.text: If it ___ been for her coach's support, she would have given up skating.

questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'take something into account': Take the cost into account.

wrongReasons.put: 'put into account' is wrong; the phrase is 'take into account'.
wrongReasons.have: 'have into account' is not English; use 'take into account'.

questions.text: We need to ___ into account the needs of elderly passengers.

questions.explanation: 'Please find attached/enclosed' is a fixed formal phrase in letters and emails: Please find attached the invoice.

wrongReasons.attach: After 'find' + object we need a past participle: 'attached'.
wrongReasons.here: 'Please find here' is not the standard formal phrase; use 'attached' or 'enclosed'.

questions.text: Please find ___ a copy of my CV.

questions.explanation: 'Having been + past participle' is a passive participle clause for an earlier action: Having been told, she agreed.

wrongReasons.being: 'Being been' is not grammatical; we need 'Having been'.
wrongReasons.had: 'Had been warned' without a subject is not a complete clause; use 'Having'.

questions.text: ___ been warned about the storm, the sailors stayed in port.

questions.explanation: 'Only after' + clause at the start causes inversion in the main clause: Only after lunch did we leave.

wrongReasons.had: 'had' would need 'withdrawn', but the verb is the base form 'withdraw'.
wrongReasons.were: 'were' would need an -ing or passive form; with the base form 'withdraw' we use 'did'.

questions.text: Only after the treaty had been signed ___ the two armies withdraw from the border.

questions.explanation: After 'The reason' we use 'why' or 'that' to introduce the clause: The reason why I called is simple.

wrongReasons.because: 'The reason because' is wrong; we say 'The reason why/that'.
wrongReasons.for: 'The reason for' is followed by a noun, not by a clause with a subject and verb.

questions.text: The reason ___ I left the company was the lack of training.

questions.explanation: 'If it were not for + noun' means 'without' in the present: If it were not for work, I would travel.

wrongReasons.is: The condition is unreal ('could play'), so we need a past form like 'were'.
wrongReasons.had: 'If it had not for' is wrong; the past form needs 'had not been for'.

questions.text: If it ___ not for the rain, we could play outside.

questions.explanation: We say 'do harm/damage to someone': Smoking does you harm.

wrongReasons.made: We don't 'make harm'; the verb is 'do'.
wrongReasons.caused: 'cause harm' is fine, but not with two objects ('caused the reputation harm'); here we need 'did'.

questions.text: The scandal ___ the minister's reputation irreparable harm.

questions.explanation: 'Upon/On receipt of' is a formal way to say 'when we receive': Tickets are sent on receipt of payment.

wrongReasons.after: 'after receipt of' is understandable, but the fixed formal phrase is 'upon receipt of'.
wrongReasons.at: 'at receipt of' is not used; say 'on' or 'upon receipt of'.

questions.text: Your order will be dispatched ___ receipt of payment.

questions.explanation: A past participle can replace a passive relative clause: The documents found (= which were found).

wrongReasons.finding: The documents did not find anything; the meaning is passive, so use 'found'.
wrongReasons.founded: 'founded' comes from 'found' (= to start an organisation); the past participle of 'find' is 'found'.

questions.text: The documents ___ at the scene were sent to the laboratory.

questions.explanation: 'Little' at the start means 'not at all' and causes inversion: Little did I suspect the truth.

wrongReasons.do: The story is in the past ('was being recorded'), so the auxiliary must be past: 'did'.
wrongReasons.had: 'had' needs a past participle (known), but the verb here is the base form 'know'.

questions.text: Little ___ they know that their conversation was being recorded.

questions.explanation: 'What happened was that + clause' is a common wh-cleft to focus on an event: What happened was that we got lost.

wrongReasons.is: The event is in the past ('was cancelled'), so we need 'was'.
wrongReasons.were: A 'What' clause is singular, so the verb is 'was', not 'were'.

questions.text: What happened ___ that the ferry was cancelled because of high winds.

questions.explanation: 'Supposing' works like 'if' and here takes a past form for an imaginary situation: Supposing you lost your job, what would you do?

wrongReasons.win: With 'would' in the main clause the imaginary condition needs a past form: 'won'.
wrongReasons.would win: 'would' is not used in the condition after 'Supposing'.

questions.text: Supposing you ___ the lottery, what would you do with the money?

questions.explanation: We 'shed/throw light on' something to explain it: The study sheds light on sleep.

wrongReasons.gives: 'give light on' is not a collocation; we say 'shed light on'.
wrongReasons.puts: 'put light on' is not used with this meaning; use 'shed light on'.

questions.text: The research ___ new light on the causes of the disease.

questions.explanation: 'Please do not hesitate to contact us' is a fixed formal closing: Do not hesitate to ask.

wrongReasons.doubt: 'doubt to contact' is not English; the formal phrase is 'do not hesitate to'.
wrongReasons.wait: 'do not wait to contact us' changes the meaning; the fixed formal phrase uses 'hesitate'.

questions.text: Should you require any further assistance, please do not ___ to contact us.

questions.explanation: A past participle clause has a passive meaning: Seen from above = When it is seen from above.

wrongReasons.seeing: The mountain does not see anything; the meaning is passive, so use 'Seen'.
wrongReasons.saw: 'saw' is a past tense form and cannot start a participle clause.

questions.text: ___ from a distance, the mountain looks like a sleeping giant.

questions.explanation: When 'Not until' + clause starts the sentence, the main clause is inverted: Not until night did it stop raining.

wrongReasons.had: After 'had' we need a past participle (sat), but the verb is the base form 'sit'.
wrongReasons.could: 'could' gives the idea of ability, which changes the meaning; the simple past inversion is 'did'.

questions.text: Not until the last guest had left ___ the hosts sit down to eat.

questions.explanation: In an it-cleft the focused part is followed by 'that' (or 'which' for things): It is the noise that bothers me.

wrongReasons.what: 'what' already contains its own noun ('the thing that'); after 'the lack of sleep' we need 'that'.
wrongReasons.who: 'who' is for people, but the focus here is 'the lack of sleep'.

questions.text: It is the lack of sleep, not the workload, ___ makes me so tired.

questions.explanation: 'If you should' makes a condition more tentative and polite: If you should see him, say hello.

wrongReasons.would: 'would' is normally not used in the if-clause; to sound tentative we use 'should'.
wrongReasons.will: 'If you will come across' is wrong for a simple future condition; use 'should' or the present.

questions.text: If you ___ come across my keys, please let me know.

questions.explanation: The collocation is 'play a role/part in': Luck played a role in our win.

wrongReasons.made: We don't 'make a role'; the verb is 'play'.
wrongReasons.did: 'do a role' is wrong; we 'play a role'.

questions.text: Several factors ___ a key role in the success of the campaign.

questions.explanation: 'Until further notice' means until we tell you something new: The office is closed until further notice.

wrongReasons.to: 'to further notice' is wrong; the fixed phrase is 'until further notice'.
wrongReasons.for: 'for further notice' is not English; use 'until further notice'.

questions.text: The meeting has been postponed ___ further notice.

questions.explanation: A present participle can replace an active relative clause: Anyone wishing to join (= who wishes to join).

wrongReasons.wishes: 'Anyone wishes' needs 'who' (Anyone who wishes); without it we use 'wishing'.
wrongReasons.wished: 'wished' would make the meaning passive or past, which does not fit.

questions.text: Anyone ___ to attend the conference should register before Friday.

questions.explanation: 'Rarely' at the start causes inversion; 'in recent years' needs the present perfect: Rarely has it snowed so much lately.

wrongReasons.did: 'did' needs a base form, but 'admitted' here is a past participle.
wrongReasons.had: 'in recent years' links the past to now, so we need 'has', not the past perfect 'had'.

questions.text: Rarely ___ a politician admitted a mistake so openly in recent years.

questions.explanation: A wh-cleft is followed by a singular verb that matches the tense: What they found was a key.

wrongReasons.were: A 'What' clause takes a singular verb, so we need 'was'.
wrongReasons.it was: The 'What' clause is already the subject, so adding 'it' creates two subjects.

questions.text: What the scientists discovered ___ a completely new species of frog.

questions.explanation: 'As long as' means 'on condition that': As long as you are careful, you can go.

wrongReasons.that: 'As long that' is not a correct phrase; it is 'as long as'.
wrongReasons.like: 'As long like' is incorrect; the expression is 'as long as'.

questions.text: As long ___ you return the car by Friday, you can borrow it.

questions.explanation: 'Come under criticism/fire' means to be criticised: The plan came under criticism.

wrongReasons.critics: 'critics' are people; after 'come under' we need the noun 'criticism'.
wrongReasons.criticise: After the adjective 'heavy' we need a noun, not a verb.

questions.text: The airline has come under heavy ___ for cancelling hundreds of flights without warning.

questions.explanation: 'may have + past participle' talks about a possible past effect: This may have caused delays.

wrongReasons.has: After the modal 'may' we always use the base form 'have'.
wrongReasons.had: After 'may' we need the base form, not the past 'had'.

questions.text: We regret any delay that this change may ___ caused to your travel plans.

questions.explanation: 'Having' is followed by a past participle: Having seen the film, I ...

wrongReasons.reading: After 'Having' we need a past participle, not the -ing form.
wrongReasons.readed: 'read' is irregular: its past participle is 'read', not 'readed'.

questions.text: Having ___ the instructions twice, I still couldn't assemble the desk.

questions.explanation: 'Should you' + base form is a formal way to say 'If you have': Should you need help, call us.

wrongReasons.had: After 'Should' we always use the base form of the verb, not the past.
wrongReasons.having: 'Should' is a modal verb and must be followed by a base form, not an -ing form.

questions.text: Should you ___ any further questions, please contact our support team.

questions.explanation: 'It was only when ... that' is an it-cleft focusing on time: It was only when he left that I cried.

wrongReasons.when: 'when' already appears in the focused part; the cleft is completed with 'that'.
wrongReasons.then: 'then' is an adverb and cannot link the two clauses in this pattern.

questions.text: It was only when I read the letter ___ I understood her decision.

questions.explanation: A mixed conditional uses a past condition with a present result: If I had moved, I would be living there now.

wrongReasons.would have: 'now' shows a present result, so we need 'would be living', not 'would have'.
wrongReasons.will: The condition is unreal, so 'will' is wrong; we need 'would'.

questions.text: If he had taken the job in Tokyo, he ___ be living in Japan now.

questions.explanation: We always say 'pay attention to': Pay attention to the signs.

wrongReasons.make: We don't 'make attention'; the verb is 'pay'.
wrongReasons.give: 'give attention to' is possible in some contexts, but the fixed instruction is 'pay attention to'.

questions.text: Please ___ attention to the safety instructions before the flight takes off.

questions.explanation: We say 'responsibility for something': She took responsibility for the error.

wrongReasons.of: 'responsibility of' refers to whose duty it is, not to the thing; here we need 'for'.
wrongReasons.about: 'responsibility about' is not used; the preposition is 'for'.

questions.text: The hotel accepts no responsibility ___ items left in the rooms.

questions.explanation: A past participle clause can describe a feeling caused by something: Shocked by the news, he sat down.

wrongReasons.delighting: 'delighting' means causing delight; the students felt it, so use 'delighted'.
wrongReasons.delight: 'delight' is a noun or base verb; we need the participle 'delighted'.

questions.text: The students, ___ by the results, celebrated late into the night.

questions.explanation: In a third conditional we can drop 'if' and invert: Had I known = If I had known.

wrongReasons.if: 'If I known' is wrong: with 'if' we would also need 'had' (If I had known). The inverted form is 'Had I known'.
wrongReasons.would: 'would' belongs in the result clause; the condition needs 'Had'.

questions.text: ___ I known about the traffic, I would have taken the train.

questions.explanation: An it-cleft starts with 'It is/was' + focus + 'that': It was the dog that barked.

wrongReasons.what: 'What was the noise' turns it into a question; the cleft needs 'It'.
wrongReasons.that: The cleft structure begins with 'It', and 'that' comes later in the sentence.

questions.text: ___ was a tiny mistake in the calculations that caused the rocket to fail.

questions.explanation: 'On condition that' means 'only if': You can come on condition that you are quiet.

wrongReasons.if: 'on condition if' is wrong; the fixed phrase is 'on condition that'.
wrongReasons.which: 'which' cannot introduce this kind of condition; we need 'that'.

questions.text: I'll lend you the money on condition ___ you pay me back next month.

questions.explanation: We 'reach' or 'sign' an agreement: The unions reached an agreement.

wrongReasons.arrived: 'arrive' needs 'at' (arrive at an agreement); without it the sentence is wrong.
wrongReasons.did: We don't 'do an agreement'; use 'reach' or 'sign'.

questions.text: The two countries finally ___ an agreement after months of negotiation.

questions.explanation: 'No later than' sets a final deadline: Reply no later than Friday.

wrongReasons.late: After 'no' and before 'than' we need the comparative 'later'.
wrongReasons.more: 'no more than' is about quantity, not about a deadline.

questions.text: Applicants must submit their forms no ___ than 30 June.

questions.explanation: 'Having + past participle' shows a cause that happened before: Having grown up there, he knew the area.

wrongReasons.being: 'Being lived' is not grammatical; we need 'Having lived'.
wrongReasons.had: 'Had lived' without a subject is not a correct clause; use 'Having'.

questions.text: ___ lived abroad for many years, she found it hard to readjust to life at home.

questions.explanation: 'Were + subject + to-infinitive' is a formal inverted condition: Were he to resign = If he resigned.

wrongReasons.was: In this formal inverted condition only 'were' is used, even with a singular subject.
wrongReasons.if: 'If the council to close' has no verb; we need the inversion 'Were the council to close'.

questions.text: ___ the council to close the library, many elderly residents would lose a vital service.

questions.explanation: After a wh-cleft with 'do', we use 'is' + (to) base form: What you need to do is rest.

wrongReasons.are: A 'What' clause takes a singular verb, so 'is' is correct.
wrongReasons.was: The advice is about now ('should'), so the present 'is' is needed.

questions.text: What you should do ___ speak to your manager directly.

questions.explanation: 'Were I' is a formal inverted form of 'If I were', followed by 'would' + base form: Were I rich, I would travel.

wrongReasons.will: The condition is imaginary ('Were I'), so 'will' does not fit; use 'would'.
wrongReasons.had: 'had think' is not correct; the result clause needs 'would' + base form.

questions.text: Were I in your position, I ___ think twice before signing the contract.

questions.explanation: A law 'comes into force/effect' when it starts to apply: The rule came into force in May.

wrongReasons.power: People come to power, but laws come into 'force'.
wrongReasons.action: 'come into action' is not used for laws; we say 'come into force'.

questions.text: The ban on single-use plastics will come into ___ at the start of next year.

questions.explanation: 'In view of / In light of' means 'because of' in formal English: In view of the cost, we cancelled.

wrongReasons.spite: 'In spite of' means 'although', which gives the wrong meaning here.
wrongReasons.case: 'In case of' means 'if something happens', not 'because of'.

questions.text: In ___ of the bad weather, the ceremony will be held indoors.

questions.explanation: A past participle can replace a passive relative clause: The paintings shown (= which are shown).

wrongReasons.showed: 'showed' is a past tense form; we need the past participle 'shown'.
wrongReasons.display: 'display' is a base form; we need the participle 'displayed'.

questions.text: All the paintings ___ in the exhibition were painted by local artists.

questions.explanation: 'Only in + time phrase' at the start causes inversion; 'in recent years' needs the present perfect: Only recently have I noticed it.

wrongReasons.did: 'started' here is a past participle after the auxiliary, so it needs 'have', not 'did'.
wrongReasons.had: 'in recent years' reaches up to now, so the present perfect 'have' is needed.

questions.text: Only in recent years ___ economists started to measure wellbeing as well as income.

questions.explanation: 'The person who/that ...' introduces the subject part of a cleft-like sentence: The one who helped was Ana.

wrongReasons.which: 'which' is for things, but here we talk about a person.
wrongReasons.whose: 'whose' shows possession and must be followed by a noun.

questions.text: The person ___ deserves the credit is the project leader, not me.

questions.explanation: A third conditional uses 'would/could/might have' + past participle in the result: If you had asked, I would have helped.

wrongReasons.will: The situation is in the past and unreal, so 'will' is wrong.
wrongReasons.had: 'had have' is not correct; use 'would/could have'.

questions.text: If you had told me earlier, I ___ have booked a bigger table.

questions.explanation: 'A foregone conclusion' is a result that is certain in advance: His victory was a foregone conclusion.

wrongReasons.forgiven: 'forgiven' comes from 'forgive' and has nothing to do with certainty.
wrongReasons.finished: 'a finished conclusion' is not an English expression; it is 'a foregone conclusion'.

questions.text: It's a ___ conclusion that the merger will go ahead.

questions.explanation: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by -ing: I look forward to meeting you.

wrongReasons.work: 'to' in 'look forward to' is a preposition, so we need 'working', not the base form.
wrongReasons.worked: After the preposition 'to' we need the -ing form, not a past form.

questions.text: We look forward to ___ with you on future projects.

questions.explanation: An -ing clause can give the reason for an action: Seeing the rain, we stayed in.

wrongReasons.seen: 'Seen' is passive; we were the ones who saw, so use 'Seeing'.
wrongReasons.saw: 'Saw' is a past tense and cannot start this clause without a subject.

questions.text: ___ that the shop was closed, we went to a café instead.

questions.explanation: 'So + adjective' at the start is followed by the verb and then the subject: So cold was the water that nobody swam.

wrongReasons.were: The subject is 'the exam', which is singular, so we need 'was'.
wrongReasons.did: 'difficult' is an adjective, so the verb needed is 'be', not 'did'.

questions.text: So difficult ___ the exam that half the students failed.

questions.explanation: An it-cleft focusing on a time uses 'that' (or 'when'): It was in May that they married.

wrongReasons.which: 'which' cannot introduce a cleft focusing on a time like 'in 1969'.
wrongReasons.where: 'where' refers to a place, not to a year.

questions.text: It was in 1969 ___ humans first walked on the Moon.

questions.explanation: An inverted third conditional ('Had + subject + participle') takes 'could/would have' in the result: Had we left earlier, we could have caught it.

wrongReasons.will: The situation is past and unreal, so 'will' cannot be used.
wrongReasons.can: 'can have been avoided' does not express an unreal past; we need 'could'.

questions.text: Had the bridge been inspected properly, the accident ___ have been avoided.

questions.explanation: 'In high spirits' means happy and full of energy: The children were in high spirits.

wrongReasons.mood: We say 'in a good mood', not 'in high mood'.
wrongReasons.spirit: The fixed phrase is plural: 'in high spirits'.

questions.text: Despite the setback, the team remained in high ___ throughout the tournament.

questions.explanation: 'Reserve the right to do something' is a fixed formal phrase: We reserve the right to refuse entry.

wrongReasons.rights: The fixed phrase is singular: 'reserve the right to'.
wrongReasons.option: 'reserve the option to' is not the standard legal phrase; use 'the right'.

questions.text: The company reserves the ___ to change prices without notice.

questions.explanation: A participle can replace a relative clause: Any passenger travelling (= who travels) ...

wrongReasons.travels: 'Any passenger travels' needs 'who'; without it we use 'travelling'.
wrongReasons.travelled: 'travelled' does not fit the active meaning here; use 'travelling'.

questions.text: Any passenger ___ without a valid ticket will be fined.

questions.explanation: 'Such + be + noun phrase + that' is an emphatic inversion: Such was his anger that he left.

wrongReasons.were: The subject 'the popularity' is singular, so the verb is 'was'.
wrongReasons.is: The rest of the sentence is in the past ('extended'), so the verb must be 'was'.

questions.text: Such ___ the popularity of the exhibition that the gallery extended its opening hours.

questions.explanation: A wh-cleft in the present is followed by 'is': What worries me is the cost.

wrongReasons.are: A 'What' clause takes a singular verb, so we need 'is'.
wrongReasons.it's: 'What really annoys me' is already the subject, so 'it' is not needed.

questions.text: What really annoys me ___ the way he interrupts everyone.

questions.explanation: 'If only + past perfect' expresses regret about the past: If only I had studied harder.

wrongReasons.have: The regret is about the past ('before the prices went up'), so we need 'had'.
wrongReasons.would have: 'would' is not used after 'If only' for past regrets; use 'had'.

questions.text: If only we ___ booked the hotel earlier, before the prices went up.

questions.explanation: 'Word of mouth' means people telling each other: The café became popular by word of mouth.

wrongReasons.words: The fixed expression is singular: 'word of mouth'.
wrongReasons.talk: 'talk of mouth' is not English; the expression is 'word of mouth'.

questions.text: The charity relies heavily on ___ of mouth to attract new volunteers.

questions.explanation: 'On production/presentation of' means when you show something: Entry on presentation of a ticket.

wrongReasons.show: After 'on' we need a noun; the formal phrase is 'on production of'.
wrongReasons.producing: The fixed formal phrase uses the noun 'production', not 'producing'.

questions.text: Refunds will only be given on ___ of a valid receipt.

questions.explanation: A conjunction like 'When' can introduce a participle clause: When asked, he said no.

wrongReasons.having: 'Having asked' would mean the spokesperson asked; the meaning is passive.
wrongReasons.after: 'After asked' is wrong; we say 'after being asked' or 'when asked'.

questions.text: ___ asked about the delay, the spokesperson refused to comment.

questions.explanation: 'At no point' at the start causes inversion; with the base form we use 'did': At no point did she complain.

wrongReasons.had: 'had' would need the participle 'mentioned', but the verb here is the base form 'mention'.
wrongReasons.was: 'was' cannot be followed by the base form 'mention'.

questions.text: At no point ___ the manager mention that the job involved weekend work.

questions.explanation: A wh-cleft uses 'was' when the 'What' clause is in the past: What saved us was luck.

wrongReasons.were: A 'What' clause is singular, so the verb must be 'was'.
wrongReasons.is: 'made' is past, so the main verb should be past too: 'was'.

questions.text: What made the film so successful ___ its brilliant soundtrack.

questions.explanation: A mixed conditional uses 'If + past perfect' for a past event and 'would' for the present result: If I had woken up, I would be there now.

wrongReasons.has: The condition is unreal and past, so we need the past perfect 'had'.
wrongReasons.would have: 'would' is not used in the if-clause; use 'had left'.

questions.text: If the plane ___ left on time, we would be in Rome by now.

questions.explanation: 'Make it a rule to do something' means to always do it: I make it a rule to walk every day.

wrongReasons.does: We don't say 'do it a rule'; the phrase is 'make it a rule'.
wrongReasons.takes: 'take it a rule' is not a correct expression; use 'make it a rule'.

questions.text: She ___ it a rule never to answer work emails at the weekend.

questions.explanation: 'Strictly prohibited/forbidden' is used in formal notices: Smoking is strictly prohibited.

wrongReasons.prohibit: After 'is' we need a passive past participle: 'prohibited'.
wrongReasons.banning: 'is banning' is active and has no object here; a notice needs the passive 'prohibited'.

questions.text: Visitors are reminded that photography is strictly ___ inside the museum.

questions.explanation: An -ing clause can describe an action happening at the same time: She walked home, singing.

wrongReasons.carried: 'carried' is passive or past; I was doing the action, so use 'carrying'.
wrongReasons.carry: After the comma we need an -ing participle, not the base form.

questions.text: The bus was full, so I had to stand all the way, ___ my heavy bag.

questions.explanation: 'Nowhere' at the start causes inversion of subject and verb: Nowhere is the air cleaner.

wrongReasons.it is: The subject is already 'the problem'; adding 'it' gives two subjects.
wrongReasons.are: The subject 'the problem' is singular, so the verb must be 'is'.

questions.text: Nowhere ___ the problem more visible than in our crowded city centres today.

questions.explanation: In 'It's not X that ...' clefts we use 'that' to introduce the rest: It's not the price that matters.

wrongReasons.what: 'what' cannot follow a noun like 'the money'; the cleft needs 'that'.
wrongReasons.who: 'who' is for people, not for 'the money'.

questions.text: It's not the money ___ matters, it's the experience.

questions.explanation: 'Should + subject + base form' is a formal way to say 'If': Should it rain, we will stay in.

wrongReasons.if: 'If the price fall' is wrong because it needs 'falls'; with the base form we use 'Should'.
wrongReasons.would: 'Would the price fall' is a question form, not a condition.

questions.text: ___ the price fall below ten dollars, we will buy more shares.

questions.explanation: We 'reach', 'draw' or 'come to' a conclusion: We reached the same conclusion.

wrongReasons.made: 'make a conclusion' is not the natural collocation; we 'reach' or 'draw' one.
wrongReasons.did: We don't 'do a conclusion'; use 'reach' or 'draw'.

questions.text: The two scientists ___ the same conclusion independently.

questions.explanation: 'We are in receipt of' is a formal way to say 'We have received': We are in receipt of your payment.

wrongReasons.on: 'on receipt of' means 'when we receive'; to say we have received it, use 'in receipt of'.
wrongReasons.at: 'at receipt of' is not English; the phrase is 'in receipt of'.

questions.text: We are ___ receipt of your letter dated 3 May.

questions.explanation: 'Having been + past participle' gives a passive reason that happened earlier: Having been repaired, the car ran well.

wrongReasons.being: 'Being been' is not grammatical; we need 'Having been'.
wrongReasons.has: 'Has been abandoned' without a subject is not a correct clause; use 'Having'.

questions.text: ___ been abandoned for decades, the house was in terrible condition.

questions.explanation: 'Not once' at the start causes inversion; 'he has caused' shows the present perfect: Not once has she called me.

wrongReasons.did: 'did' needs a base form, but 'apologised' here is a past participle.
wrongReasons.had: The rest of the sentence uses 'has caused', so the present perfect 'has' fits, not 'had'.

questions.text: Not once ___ he apologised for the damage he has caused.

questions.explanation: After a wh-cleft with 'do', we use 'was' + (to) base form: What I did was leave.

wrongReasons.were: A 'What' clause is singular, so we use 'was'.
wrongReasons.is: The action happened in the past ('did'), so the verb must be 'was'.

questions.text: What we did next ___ call the police.

questions.explanation: 'If you happen to' is used for a chance event: If you happen to pass a shop, buy milk.

wrongReasons.would happen: 'would' is not normally used in the if-clause; use 'happen'.
wrongReasons.will: 'If you will to see' is not grammatical; we need 'happen to'.

questions.text: If you ___ to see Maria, could you give her this book?

questions.explanation: We say something 'poses a threat/risk': Pollution poses a risk to health.

wrongReasons.makes: 'make a threat' means to threaten someone; for danger we say 'pose a threat'.
wrongReasons.does: We don't 'do a threat'; the verb is 'pose'.

questions.text: Antibiotic resistance ___ a growing threat to public health worldwide.

questions.explanation: 'With reference/regard to' is formal for 'about': With reference to your letter, ...

wrongReasons.regards: 'with regards to' is common in speech but is not correct formal English; use 'regard'.
wrongReasons.referring: 'With referring to' is wrong; the phrase is 'With reference to'.

questions.text: With ___ to your enquiry, I am pleased to confirm that the room is available.

questions.explanation: A present participle can replace an active relative clause: people working (= who work).

wrongReasons.worked: 'worked' gives a passive or past meaning; people do the work, so use 'working'.
wrongReasons.works: 'works' is a finite verb and cannot follow 'people' directly.

questions.text: The number of people ___ from home has risen sharply since 2020.

questions.explanation: 'Scarcely ... when' takes the past perfect with inversion: Scarcely had I closed my eyes when the baby cried.

wrongReasons.did: 'Scarcely ... when' describes one past action just before another, so it needs the past perfect 'had'.
wrongReasons.have: The waiter 'brought' the bill in the past, so the earlier action needs 'had', not 'have'.

questions.text: Scarcely ___ we sat down when the waiter brought the bill.

questions.explanation: 'The last thing / The only thing + clause' is followed by 'is/was': The only thing I want is sleep.

wrongReasons.were: The subject is 'The last thing', which is singular, so we need 'was'.
wrongReasons.is: 'expected' is past, so the main verb should be 'was'.

questions.text: The last thing I expected ___ a phone call from the director.

questions.explanation: A mixed conditional can have a negative past condition with a present result: If I hadn't met her, I wouldn't be here.

wrongReasons.didn't: The condition is about an unreal past, so we need 'hadn't acted'.
wrongReasons.haven't: The present perfect does not fit an unreal past condition; use 'hadn't'.

questions.text: If the doctors ___ acted so quickly, he wouldn't be alive today.

questions.explanation: 'Rave reviews' are extremely positive reviews: The book got rave reviews.

wrongReasons.raving: The fixed collocation is 'rave reviews', not 'raving reviews'.
wrongReasons.raved: 'raved' is a past verb form; before 'reviews' we need 'rave'.

questions.text: The actor's performance received ___ reviews from critics across the country.

questions.explanation: 'Be subject/liable to' means it may happen to you: Prices are subject to change.

wrongReasons.object: 'be object to' is wrong; you may 'object to' something, but here we need 'subject'.
wrongReasons.exposing: 'be exposing to' is not grammatical; the formal phrase is 'be subject to'.

questions.text: Students who fail to attend will be ___ to disciplinary action.

questions.explanation: A past participle clause has a passive meaning: Written by experts = It was written by experts.

wrongReasons.writing: The book did not write anything; the meaning is passive, so use 'Written'.
wrongReasons.wrote: 'wrote' is the past tense; the past participle is 'written'.

questions.text: ___ in simple language, the book is ideal for young readers.

questions.explanation: A negative object like 'Not a single word' at the start causes inversion with 'did' + base form: Not a single mistake did he make.

wrongReasons.had: 'had' needs the participle 'received', but the verb here is 'receive'.
wrongReasons.was: 'was' cannot be followed by the base form 'receive'.

questions.text: Not a single complaint ___ the hotel receive during its first year.

questions.explanation: In an it-cleft the focused quality is followed by 'that' (or 'which'): It was his patience that helped.

wrongReasons.what: After a focused noun like 'her honesty' we need 'that', not 'what'.
wrongReasons.who: 'who' refers to a person, but the focus is 'her honesty'.

questions.text: It was her honesty, more than her experience, ___ impressed the interview panel.

questions.explanation: 'Without + noun' can replace an if-clause and is followed by 'would': Without water, plants would die.

wrongReasons.will: The situation is imaginary, so we need 'would', not 'will'.
wrongReasons.is: 'is be' is not grammatical; we need a modal like 'would'.

questions.text: Without the internet, modern banking ___ be impossible.

questions.explanation: 'Rise to the challenge' means to deal with a difficult situation successfully: She rose to the challenge.

wrongReasons.raised: 'raise' needs an object (raise your hand); the intransitive verb here is 'rise', past 'rose'.
wrongReasons.arose: 'arise' means 'appear or happen'; the fixed phrase is 'rise to the challenge'.

questions.text: He ___ to the challenge and finished the marathon despite his injury.

questions.explanation: 'On behalf of' means 'representing': I speak on behalf of the staff.

wrongReasons.part: 'On part of' is wrong; we say 'on the part of' or 'on behalf of'.
wrongReasons.name: 'On name of' is not English; the phrase is 'on behalf of' or 'in the name of'.

questions.text: On ___ of the whole team, I would like to thank you for your support.

questions.explanation: 'Weather permitting' is a fixed absolute participle phrase meaning 'if the weather is good': We'll eat outside, weather permitting.

wrongReasons.permitted: The fixed phrase uses the -ing form: 'weather permitting'.
wrongReasons.permits: A finite verb ('permits') would need 'if'; the fixed phrase is 'weather permitting'.

questions.text: Weather ___, the race will start at noon.

questions.explanation: 'On no account' at the start causes inversion, usually with a modal: On no account should you touch the wire.

wrongReasons.not: 'On no account' is already negative; adding 'not' creates a double negative.
wrongReasons.you should: In this inversion the auxiliary comes before the subject, and 'you' is already in the sentence.

questions.text: On no account ___ you open this door while the machine is running.

questions.explanation: A wh-clause like 'Why she resigned' acts as a singular subject: Why he left is unclear.

wrongReasons.are: A wh-clause used as a subject is singular, so the verb must be 'is'.
wrongReasons.it is: 'Why she resigned so suddenly' is already the subject, so 'it' is not needed.

questions.text: Why she resigned so suddenly ___ still a mystery to everyone.

questions.explanation: 'Assuming (that)' means 'if we accept that': Assuming that it's open, we'll go.

wrongReasons.if: 'Assuming if' is wrong; we say 'assuming that'.
wrongReasons.what: 'Assuming what' does not introduce a condition; use 'that'.

questions.text: Assuming ___ the train is on time, we'll arrive before dinner.

questions.explanation: 'Turn a blind eye to' means to ignore something wrong on purpose: The police turned a blind eye.

wrongReasons.closing: 'close a blind eye' is not the idiom; we say 'turn a blind eye'.
wrongReasons.making: 'make a blind eye' is wrong; the verb in this idiom is 'turn'.

questions.text: The politician was accused of ___ a blind eye to corruption in his party.

questions.explanation: 'For the duration of' means for the whole time: Stay seated for the duration of the flight.

wrongReasons.during: 'during the duration' repeats the same idea; we say 'for the duration of'.
wrongReasons.along: 'along' is about movement in space, not time.

questions.text: Customers are advised to retain their tickets ___ the duration of the journey.

questions.explanation: 'All things considered' is a fixed participle phrase meaning 'after thinking about everything': All things considered, it went well.

wrongReasons.considering: The fixed phrase uses the past participle: 'All things considered'.
wrongReasons.consider: We need the past participle 'considered', not the base form.

questions.text: All things ___, the conference was a great success.

questions.explanation: 'Only then' at the start causes inversion with 'did' + base form: Only then did we understand.

wrongReasons.had: 'had' would need the participle 'realised', but the verb is the base form 'realise'.
wrongReasons.do: The context is in the past ('had missed'), so the auxiliary must be 'did'.

questions.text: Only then ___ I realise how much I had missed my family.

questions.explanation: An it-cleft that focuses on a group uses 'that' (or 'who'): It is the council that decides.

wrongReasons.which: In an it-cleft about an organisation acting like people, 'that' or 'who' is used, not 'which'.
wrongReasons.what: 'what' cannot follow a noun like 'the government' in a cleft.

questions.text: It is the government ___ should take responsibility for the delays.

questions.explanation: 'If + were to + base form' describes an imaginary future action: If I were to move, I would miss you.

wrongReasons.told: After 'were to' we need the base form 'tell', not the past.
wrongReasons.telling: After 'to' we need the base form 'tell', not the -ing form.

questions.text: If I were to ___ you the truth, you wouldn't believe me.

questions.explanation: Things 'come' or 'grind' to a standstill when they stop completely: Traffic came to a standstill.

wrongReasons.went: We don't say 'go to a standstill'; use 'come to a standstill'.
wrongReasons.stopped: 'stopped to a standstill' repeats the idea and is not the collocation.

questions.text: The negotiations ___ to a standstill when neither side would compromise.

questions.explanation: 'Be pleased/delighted to announce' is a formal fixed phrase: We are pleased to announce our new office.

wrongReasons.pleasing: 'pleasing' describes something that gives pleasure; the board feels 'pleased'.
wrongReasons.pleasure: 'pleasure' is a noun; after 'is' and before 'to announce' we need an adjective.

questions.text: The board of directors is ___ to announce the appointment of a new chief executive.

questions.explanation: An -ing clause can give the reason for an action: Feeling ill, she stayed home.

wrongReasons.felt: 'Felt' is a past tense form and cannot start this clause without a subject.
wrongReasons.having feel: After 'having' we need the past participle 'felt', not the base form.

questions.text: ___ exhausted after the long flight, he went straight to bed.

questions.explanation: After 'be expected' we use a passive infinitive for a future action: The road is expected to be finished soon.

wrongReasons.being: 'expected' is followed by an infinitive, not an -ing form.
wrongReasons.to have been: 'to have been' refers to the past, but 'next year' is in the future.

questions.text: The new bridge is expected ___ completed by the end of next year.

questions.explanation: For a past action after 'is thought to' we use the perfect infinitive: He is thought to have left.

wrongReasons.has: After 'to' we need the base form 'have', not 'has'.
wrongReasons.be: 'to be fled' is not possible: 'flee' is intransitive here and the action is in the past.

questions.text: The suspect is thought to ___ fled abroad shortly after the robbery.

questions.explanation: 'Resent' is followed by an -ing form, so the passive is 'being + past participle': I resent being ignored.

wrongReasons.to be: 'resent' takes an -ing form, not an infinitive.
wrongReasons.be: After 'resent' the verb must be in the -ing form: 'being'.

questions.text: I resent ___ treated like a child by my manager.

questions.explanation: The present continuous passive is 'is/are being + past participle': The road is being repaired.

wrongReasons.been: 'is been' is not a correct form; an action in progress needs 'is being'.
wrongReasons.be: After 'is' we need 'being' for an action happening now.

questions.text: The museum's east wing is currently ___ renovated, so it is closed to visitors.

questions.explanation: The past perfect passive is 'had been + past participle': The files had been deleted.

wrongReasons.being: After 'had' we need the participle 'been', not 'being'.
wrongReasons.be: 'had be' is not a verb form; use 'had been'.

questions.text: By the time the inspectors arrived, most of the documents had already ___ destroyed.

questions.explanation: The causative 'have something done' uses the past participle: I had my hair cut.

wrongReasons.painting: The causative needs a past participle, not an -ing form.
wrongReasons.paint: The structure is 'have + object + past participle': 'painted'.

questions.text: She had her portrait ___ by a well-known local artist.

questions.explanation: 'Subject + is/was believed + to have been' reports a general belief about the past: The ship is believed to have sunk.

wrongReasons.has: 'has believed' is active; we need the passive 'is believed'.
wrongReasons.believes: The castle cannot believe anything: the structure is passive.

questions.text: The castle ___ believed to have been built in the twelfth century.

questions.explanation: After a modal the passive is 'be + past participle': Forms must be signed.

wrongReasons.been: After 'must' we use the base form 'be', not 'been'.
wrongReasons.being: A modal is followed by the base form, not an -ing form.

questions.text: All applications must ___ submitted online before the deadline.

questions.explanation: The past modal passive is 'should have been + past participle': It should have been fixed earlier.

wrongReasons.being: 'should have being' is not a correct form.

questions.text: The decision to close the factory should have ___ made months ago.

questions.explanation: 'Be likely' is followed by a to-infinitive; the passive form is 'to be + past participle': He is likely to be chosen.

wrongReasons.being: 'likely' takes a to-infinitive, not an -ing form.

questions.text: Neither of the candidates is likely ___ elected in the first round.

questions.explanation: For a past event after 'are reported' we use 'to have been + participle': They are reported to have escaped.

wrongReasons.to be: 'to be been' is impossible; the past needs 'to have been'.
wrongReasons.have: After 'reported' we need 'to' before the infinitive.

questions.text: The hostages are reported ___ been released unharmed late last night.

questions.explanation: 'Be due to' takes an infinitive; for a passive meaning we use 'to be + past participle': The report is due to be published.

wrongReasons.being: 'due' is followed by a to-infinitive, not an -ing form.
wrongReasons.to: The concert does not broadcast itself; we need the passive 'to be broadcast'.

questions.text: The concert is due ___ broadcast live on national radio.

questions.explanation: 'Not a single + singular noun' takes a singular verb: Not a single letter has arrived.

wrongReasons.have: 'a single complaint' is singular, so we need 'has'.
wrongReasons.had: 'since' with a past event links to now, so we use the present perfect 'has'.

questions.text: Not a single complaint ___ been received since the new system was introduced.

questions.explanation: 'To be being + participle' is the passive of an action in progress: He is thought to be being questioned.

wrongReasons.been: 'to be been' is not possible; an ongoing action needs 'being'.
wrongReasons.have: 'to be have' is not a verb form.

questions.text: The patient is believed to be ___ treated in intensive care.

questions.explanation: The third conditional passive uses 'would/might/could have been + participle': It would have been cancelled.

wrongReasons.will: An unreal past condition needs 'would', not 'will'.
wrongReasons.had: 'had have been' is not correct in the result clause.

questions.text: The road ___ have been closed if the storm had continued.

questions.explanation: The perfect passive participle is 'having been + participle': Having been told, she left.

wrongReasons.being: 'having being' is not a correct form.

questions.text: Having ___ warned twice, the player was sent off after a third foul.

questions.explanation: In the active 'make somebody do' has no 'to', but the passive needs 'to': They were made to wait.

wrongReasons.work: In the passive, 'make' is followed by 'to + infinitive'.
wrongReasons.working: 'were made working' is wrong; use 'were made to work'.

questions.text: The workers were made ___ overtime without extra pay.

questions.explanation: 'Wish' takes a to-infinitive; the passive is 'to be + participle': Those wishing to be included must apply.

wrongReasons.being: 'wish' is followed by a to-infinitive, not an -ing form.

questions.text: Anyone wishing ___ considered for the position should contact the office.

questions.explanation: After a preposition the passive is 'being + participle': She is tired of being watched.

wrongReasons.be: After the preposition 'about' we need an -ing form.
wrongReasons.been: 'about been' is not possible; use 'about being'.

questions.text: The singer complained about ___ followed everywhere by photographers.

questions.explanation: For a finished action at a past time we use the past simple passive: The tower was built in 1889.

wrongReasons.has been: The building finished in the past, so the present perfect does not fit.
wrongReasons.is: The action is in the past, so we need 'was'.

questions.text: The Golden Gate Bridge, which ___ built in just over four years, opened in 1937.

questions.explanation: 'Allow' and 'permit' can be used in the passive: Dogs are not allowed inside.

wrongReasons.let: 'let' is not normally used in the passive in this way.
wrongReasons.allow: After 'is not' the passive needs the past participle 'allowed'.

questions.text: Smoking is not ___ anywhere on the premises.

questions.explanation: In the active we say 'see somebody do', but in the passive 'be seen' needs 'to': She was seen to leave.

wrongReasons.for: 'was seen for climb' is not correct; the passive needs 'to + infinitive'.
wrongReasons.by: 'by' introduces the agent, not the infinitive; use 'to climb'.

questions.text: The thief was seen ___ climb over the wall at around midnight.

questions.explanation: 'Has yet to' means 'has not yet' and takes an infinitive; passive: The winner has yet to be announced.

wrongReasons.being: 'has yet' is followed by a to-infinitive, not an -ing form.
wrongReasons.been: 'has yet been' is not correct; use 'has yet to be'.

questions.text: The cause of the fire has yet ___ established.

questions.explanation: After 'insist that' formal English uses the base form (subjunctive): They insisted that he be present.

wrongReasons.was: The subjunctive uses the base form 'be', not the past 'was'.
wrongReasons.will be: After 'insist that' we use 'be' or 'should be', not 'will be'.

questions.text: The committee insisted that the report ___ rewritten before publication.

questions.explanation: After 'It is essential that' we use the base form for all persons: It is essential that she arrive on time.

wrongReasons.has: In the subjunctive the verb has no -s: 'have', not 'has'.
wrongReasons.had: The subjunctive uses the base form, not the past.

questions.text: It is essential that every passenger ___ a valid ticket.

questions.explanation: For regrets about the past we use 'wish + past perfect': I wish I had studied harder.

wrongReasons.have: A past regret needs the past perfect 'had accepted'.
wrongReasons.would have: 'wish + would have' is not used for our own past actions.

questions.text: I wish I ___ accepted that job offer in Berlin last year.

questions.explanation: 'It's high time' is followed by the past simple with present meaning: It's high time we left.

wrongReasons.does: After 'It's high time' we use the past tense, not the present.
wrongReasons.would do: 'It's high time' takes the past simple, not 'would'.

questions.text: It's high time the government ___ something about air pollution.

questions.explanation: 'If only' + past simple (or 'were') expresses a wish about the present: If only I were taller.

wrongReasons.is: A present wish after 'if only' needs a past form: 'were'.
wrongReasons.would be: 'If only she would be' is not used for an unreal present state.

questions.text: If only she ___ here now to see this!

questions.explanation: 'I'd rather + another subject' takes the past simple for present or future: I'd rather you stayed.

wrongReasons.don't: After 'I'd rather you' we use the past form 'didn't'.
wrongReasons.won't: 'would rather' with another subject is followed by the past, not 'won't'.

questions.text: I'd rather you ___ tell anyone about this yet.

questions.explanation: After 'recommend that' we use the base form or 'should + verb': They recommended that he rest.

wrongReasons.avoided: After 'recommend that' we use the base form, not the past.

questions.text: The doctor recommended that she ___ lifting heavy objects for a month.

questions.explanation: 'As though/as if' + past form shows something is not true: She acts as if she were the queen.

wrongReasons.be: After 'as though' an unreal situation needs 'were', not 'be'.
wrongReasons.has been: The idea is unreal and present, so we use the past form 'were'.

questions.text: He talks to us as though he ___ our boss, but he only joined last week.

questions.explanation: 'Suppose' + past form presents an imaginary situation, matched with 'would': Suppose you won, what would you do?

wrongReasons.will be: After 'suppose' we do not use 'will'; we use a past form.
wrongReasons.would be: 'Suppose' is followed by a past form, not 'would'.

questions.text: Suppose you ___ offered the job tomorrow — would you accept it?

questions.explanation: 'Would rather' with the same subject is followed by the bare infinitive: I'd rather walk.

wrongReasons.to take: 'would rather' takes the base form without 'to'.
wrongReasons.taking: After 'would rather' we use the base form, not -ing.

questions.text: Given the choice, I'd rather ___ the train than drive in this weather.

questions.explanation: After 'It is vital that' formal English uses the base form 'be': It is vital that the door be locked.

wrongReasons.is: In this formal structure we use the subjunctive 'be', not 'is'.
wrongReasons.are: The subjunctive form is 'be' for every subject.

questions.text: It is vital that the data ___ kept confidential.

questions.explanation: After 'demand that' we use the base form for all persons: He demanded that she leave.

wrongReasons.gave: After 'demand that' we use the base form, not the past.

questions.text: She demanded that the manager ___ her a full refund.

questions.explanation: 'Wish + would' expresses annoyance at someone's behaviour: I wish he would listen.

wrongReasons.did: 'did stop' does not express a complaint about repeated behaviour; use 'would'.

questions.text: I wish you ___ stop interrupting me when I'm speaking.

questions.explanation: 'Far be it from me' is a fixed subjunctive phrase meaning 'I don't want to': Far be it from me to complain.

wrongReasons.is: This fixed phrase uses the subjunctive 'be', not 'is'.
wrongReasons.was: The expression is always 'Far be it from me'.

questions.text: Far ___ it from me to criticise, but I think you've made a mistake.

questions.explanation: 'Come what may' is a fixed subjunctive phrase meaning 'whatever happens': Come what may, we'll stay together.

wrongReasons.will: The phrase is always 'Come what may'.

questions.text: Come what ___, I will finish this marathon.

questions.explanation: 'It's about time' + past simple suggests something should happen now: It's about time you called her.

wrongReasons.go: After 'It's about time you' we use the past form.
wrongReasons.will go: 'It's about time' is followed by the past simple, not 'will'.

questions.text: It's about time you ___ to bed — you have an exam tomorrow.

questions.explanation: After 'propose that' formal English uses 'be' or 'should be': They proposed that the plan be changed.

wrongReasons.is: After 'propose that' we use the subjunctive 'be'.
wrongReasons.was: The subjunctive is the base form 'be', not the past.

questions.text: The board proposed that the meeting ___ postponed until March.

questions.explanation: In second conditionals 'were' is used for all persons, especially in advice: If I were you, I'd go.

wrongReasons.am: An unreal condition needs a past form: 'were'.
wrongReasons.would be: We do not use 'would' in the if-clause.

questions.text: If I ___ you, I'd apologise to her straight away.

questions.explanation: 'Would rather + another subject' takes the past simple: I'd rather you cooked tonight.

wrongReasons.spend: With a different subject, 'would rather' is followed by the past: 'spent'.
wrongReasons.will spend: After 'would rather' + subject we use the past simple, not 'will'.

questions.text: She would rather her children ___ more time outdoors.

questions.explanation: After 'It is imperative that' we use the base form: It is imperative that he be told.

wrongReasons.left: This structure uses the base form, not the past.

questions.text: It is imperative that no one ___ the building until the police arrive.

questions.explanation: For a wish about an ability now we use 'wish + could': I wish I could swim.

wrongReasons.would: 'would' is not used after 'I wish I' for abilities.

questions.text: I wish I ___ speak Japanese; it would make my job much easier.

questions.explanation: 'If + were to + infinitive' presents a hypothetical future action: If he were to resign, ...

wrongReasons.going to: The structure is 'were to', not 'were going to', for a formal hypothesis.
wrongReasons.for: 'were for raise' is not correct; use 'were to raise'.

questions.text: If the government were ___ raise taxes again, there would be mass protests.

questions.explanation: 'Keep a low profile' means to avoid attention: The actor kept a low profile after the trial.

wrongReasons.level: The idiom is 'keep a low profile', not 'level'.
wrongReasons.face: 'keep a low face' is not an English expression.

questions.text: After the scandal, the minister decided to keep a low ___ for a few months.

questions.explanation: 'Hit the ground running' means to start something with great energy and success.

wrongReasons.run: The idiom uses the -ing form: 'hit the ground running'.

questions.text: The new manager really hit the ground ___ and doubled sales in her first month.

questions.explanation: 'A steep learning curve' means something that is difficult to learn quickly.

wrongReasons.line: The collocation is 'learning curve', not 'learning line'.
wrongReasons.slope: Although 'steep' suggests a hill, the expression is 'learning curve'.

questions.text: Learning to code was a steep learning ___ for me at first.

questions.explanation: 'Back to the drawing board' means starting a plan again after it failed.

wrongReasons.table: The idiom is 'drawing board', not 'drawing table'.
wrongReasons.paper: 'back to the drawing paper' is not the fixed expression.

questions.text: We'll have to go back to the drawing ___ — the client rejected all our designs.

questions.explanation: 'Neck and neck' means level in a competition, with neither ahead.

wrongReasons.head: The expression repeats the same word: 'neck and neck'.
wrongReasons.shoulder: 'shoulder to shoulder' means side by side, but this idiom is 'neck and neck'.

questions.text: The two candidates are neck and ___ in the latest polls.

questions.explanation: 'Burn your bridges' means to destroy a relationship so you cannot go back.

wrongReasons.boats: 'burn your boats' means to commit yourself, not to damage a relationship.
wrongReasons.bridge: The idiom uses the plural: 'burn your bridges'.

questions.text: I know you're upset, but try not to burn your ___ with the company; you might want to work there again.

questions.explanation: 'Burn the candle at both ends' means to work very hard and rest too little.

wrongReasons.sides: A candle has two ends, and the idiom is 'at both ends'.

questions.text: She's been working all hours, burning the candle at both ___.

questions.explanation: 'A drop in the ocean' (American: 'in the bucket') means an amount far too small to make a difference.

wrongReasons.sea: The fixed idiom is 'a drop in the ocean', not 'in the sea'.
wrongReasons.water: 'a drop in the water' is not an idiom; we say 'a drop in the ocean'.

questions.text: Their donation was a drop in the ___ compared with what the hospital actually needs.

questions.explanation: 'Back on track' means making progress as planned again.

wrongReasons.road: The idiom is 'back on track', not 'on road'.
wrongReasons.line: 'back on line' does not mean 'progressing as planned'.

questions.text: The project is finally back on ___ after months of delays.

questions.explanation: 'Give someone the cold shoulder' means to ignore them deliberately.

wrongReasons.cool: The fixed idiom is 'cold shoulder', not 'cool shoulder'.
wrongReasons.frozen: 'frozen shoulder' is a medical condition, not this idiom.

questions.text: He was given the ___ shoulder by his colleagues after he reported them.

questions.explanation: 'Beat about the bush' means to avoid saying something directly.

wrongReasons.tree: The idiom is 'beat about the bush', not 'the tree'.
wrongReasons.point: You can 'get to the point', but you 'beat about the bush'.

questions.text: Let's not beat about the ___: the company is losing money.

questions.explanation: 'Hit the nail on the head' means to describe exactly what is causing a problem.

wrongReasons.top: The idiom refers to the 'head' of the nail.
wrongReasons.point: The fixed expression is 'on the head', not 'on the point'.

questions.text: You hit the nail on the ___ when you said the problem was poor communication.

questions.explanation: 'At the eleventh hour' means at the last possible moment.

wrongReasons.minute: We say 'at the last minute' but 'at the eleventh hour'.
wrongReasons.moment: 'the eleventh moment' is not an English expression.

questions.text: The deal fell through at the eleventh ___, just before it was due to be signed.

questions.explanation: 'Be in two minds' means to be unable to decide.

wrongReasons.thoughts: The idiom is 'in two minds', not 'in two thoughts'.

questions.text: I'm in two ___ about whether to accept the offer.

questions.explanation: 'Red tape' means too many official rules and forms that cause delay.

wrongReasons.lines: The idiom for bureaucracy is 'red tape'.
wrongReasons.paper: 'red paper' does not describe bureaucracy; the expression is 'red tape'.

questions.text: Getting the building permit took ages because of all the red ___.

questions.explanation: 'No mean feat' means a considerable achievement.

wrongReasons.fit: 'fit' sounds similar, but the noun meaning 'achievement' is 'feat'.
wrongReasons.effort: The fixed expression is 'no mean feat'.

questions.text: Running a marathon was no mean ___ for someone who only started training in spring.

questions.explanation: 'You could hear a pin drop' means the room was completely silent.

wrongReasons.falling: After 'heard a pin' the idiom uses the base form 'drop'.

questions.text: When the boss announced the cuts, you could have heard a pin ___.

questions.explanation: 'Jump to conclusions' means to decide something too quickly without the facts.

wrongReasons.decisions: The idiom is 'jump to conclusions', not 'decisions'.

questions.text: The spokesperson warned journalists not to jump to ___ before the investigation was complete.

questions.explanation: 'Take something with a pinch of salt' means not to believe it completely.

wrongReasons.sugar: The idiom is 'a pinch of salt'; sugar has no such meaning.
wrongReasons.pepper: 'a pinch of pepper' is literal cooking, not an idiom about doubt.

questions.text: He tends to exaggerate, so I'd take his stories with a pinch of ___.

questions.explanation: 'A white elephant' is something expensive that is useless or unwanted.

wrongReasons.horse: A 'white horse' has no idiomatic meaning here.
wrongReasons.whale: The idiom for a costly useless thing is 'white elephant'.

questions.text: The new stadium has become a white ___: nobody uses it and it costs a fortune to maintain.

questions.explanation: 'A leap in the dark' means an action whose result you cannot predict.

wrongReasons.air: The idiom is 'a leap in the dark', not 'in the air'.

questions.text: Leaving a secure job to start my own business was a real leap in the ___.

questions.explanation: 'Open a can of worms' means to create a complicated new problem.

wrongReasons.beans: 'a can of beans' has no idiomatic meaning here.
wrongReasons.snakes: The idiom is 'a can of worms'.

questions.text: Questioning the old contract opened a can of ___ that nobody wanted to deal with.

questions.explanation: 'Put off' or 'put back' means to postpone: They put off the wedding.

wrongReasons.away: 'put away' means to store something, not to postpone.
wrongReasons.out: 'put out' means to extinguish or to inconvenience someone.

questions.text: Because of the strike, the meeting has been put ___ until next Thursday.

questions.explanation: 'Figure out' means to understand or solve: I can't figure out this puzzle.

wrongReasons.up: 'figure up' is not used to mean 'understand'.
wrongReasons.off: 'figure off' is not an English phrasal verb.

questions.text: Nobody could figure ___ how the thieves had got into the vault.

questions.explanation: 'Lay off' means to stop employing workers because there is not enough work.

wrongReasons.down: 'lay down' means to establish rules or put something down.
wrongReasons.out: 'lay out' means to arrange or spend money, not to dismiss staff.

questions.text: The company was forced to lay ___ two hundred workers.

questions.explanation: 'Come up with' means to think of an idea or plan.

wrongReasons.out: 'come out with' means to say something suddenly, not to invent a solution.
wrongReasons.across: 'come across' means to find by chance and is not followed by 'with'.

questions.text: She came ___ with a brilliant solution to the storage problem.

questions.explanation: 'Break down' (fail) or 'break off' (end suddenly) can describe talks.

wrongReasons.out: 'break out' is used for wars, fires or diseases starting.

questions.text: The negotiations broke ___ after the union rejected the final offer.

questions.explanation: 'Put up with' means to tolerate: She puts up with a lot.

wrongReasons.off: 'put off with' is not a phrasal verb; 'put off' means postpone.
wrongReasons.down: 'put down' means to criticise or place something down.

questions.text: I can't put ___ with this noise any longer.

questions.explanation: 'Crack down on' means to deal with something illegal more strictly.

wrongReasons.up: 'crack up' means to laugh a lot or have a breakdown.
wrongReasons.off: 'crack off' is not used with this meaning.

questions.text: The government has pledged to crack ___ on tax evasion.

questions.explanation: 'Get over' means to recover from something unpleasant.

wrongReasons.off: 'get off' means to leave a vehicle or avoid punishment.
wrongReasons.by: 'get by' means to manage with little money.

questions.text: It took her months to get ___ the shock of losing her job.

questions.explanation: 'Turn out' means to prove to be: The film turned out to be great.

wrongReasons.up: 'turn up' means to arrive or appear.
wrongReasons.over: 'turn over' means to flip something, not to prove to be.

questions.text: The rumours about the merger turned ___ to be completely true.

questions.explanation: 'Phase out' means to remove gradually; 'phase in' means to introduce gradually.

wrongReasons.off: 'phase off' is not an English phrasal verb.
wrongReasons.away: The correct particles with 'phase' are 'in' and 'out'.

questions.text: The old tax scheme was phased ___ gradually over a period of five years.

questions.explanation: 'Go on (about)' means to talk for a long time about something.

wrongReasons.over: 'go over' means to review or check something.
wrongReasons.off: 'go off' means to explode, ring, or go bad.

questions.text: The lecturer went ___ about her research for so long that we missed the bus.

questions.explanation: 'Piece together' means to discover the truth from separate pieces of information.

wrongReasons.up: 'piece up' is not an English phrasal verb.
wrongReasons.out: We say 'work out' or 'figure out', but 'piece together'.

questions.text: Investigators are still trying to piece ___ what happened on the night of the crash.

questions.explanation: 'Go off' is used for alarms ringing suddenly: My alarm went off at six.

wrongReasons.on: 'go on' means to continue, not to start ringing.
wrongReasons.out: 'go out' is used for lights or fires stopping.

questions.text: The fire alarm went ___ in the middle of the exam.

questions.explanation: 'Hand out' means to give something to each person in a group.

wrongReasons.off: 'hand off' is a sports term, not 'distribute'.
wrongReasons.up: 'hand up' is not used to mean 'distribute'.

questions.text: The charity relies on volunteers to hand ___ food to homeless people.

questions.explanation: 'Pick up' can mean to improve: Business is picking up.

wrongReasons.on: 'pick on' means to treat someone unfairly.
wrongReasons.out: 'pick out' means to choose or recognise.

questions.text: Sales have picked ___ considerably since the new advertising campaign.

questions.explanation: 'Back down (on)' means to withdraw a claim or promise under pressure.

wrongReasons.up: 'back up' means to support someone or copy data.
wrongReasons.off: 'back off' means to move away or stop pressuring someone.

questions.text: Faced with public anger, the minister was forced to back ___ on her promise to cut taxes.

questions.explanation: 'Fill somebody in' means to give them information they missed.

wrongReasons.up: 'fill up' means to make something full.
wrongReasons.on: 'fill on' is not a phrasal verb; the particle is 'in', followed by 'on'.

questions.text: Could you fill me ___ on what was decided at the meeting?

questions.explanation: 'Look into' means to investigate: We'll look into the matter.

wrongReasons.after: 'look after' means to take care of someone.
wrongReasons.for: 'look for' means to search for something lost.

questions.text: The police are looking ___ the complaint and will report back next week.

questions.explanation: 'Come out' means to be published or released: The album came out in May.

wrongReasons.up: 'come up' means to be mentioned or to arise.
wrongReasons.off: 'come off' means to succeed or become detached.

questions.text: Her new novel comes ___ in paperback next month.

questions.explanation: 'Cut back on' and 'cut down on' mean to reduce: Cut down on sugar.

wrongReasons.off: 'cut off' means to disconnect or isolate.
wrongReasons.out: 'cut out' means to stop completely or remove.

questions.text: We need to cut ___ on unnecessary spending.

questions.explanation: 'Make up' means to invent a story or excuse.

wrongReasons.out: 'make out' means to see with difficulty or understand.

questions.text: The witness later admitted that he had made ___ the entire story.

questions.explanation: 'Hold up' means to delay: Sorry, I was held up at work.

wrongReasons.on: 'hold on' means to wait or grip firmly.
wrongReasons.down: 'hold down' means to keep a job or keep something low.

questions.text: An accident on the motorway held ___ the traffic for hours.

questions.explanation: 'Despite' and 'in spite of' are followed by a noun or -ing form: Despite the cold, we swam.
